name: Elif's skin in the cold and the snow-glare

parameters.label: Hours outside
parameters.explain: Sun damage adds up with time outdoors; the redness shows up hours afterwards.

parameters.label: UV index
parameters.explain: The UV index measures how strong the sun's UV is; at 3 or more, skin needs protection.

parameters.label: Ground
parameters.explain: Snow reflects up to 80% of the sun's UV, so the rays hit you twice — from above and from below.

parameters.label: Face protection
parameters.explain: Sunscreen blocks much of the UV before it reaches the skin cells.

parameters.label: Air temperature
parameters.explain: The colder the air, the faster it pulls heat from exposed skin.

parameters.label: Wind
parameters.explain: Wind makes heat leave exposed skin faster — that's what the 'wind chill' temperature measures.

parameters.label: How easily her skin burns
parameters.explain: People's skin differs in how much UV it takes before it burns.

parameters.label: Clothing
parameters.explain: Warm, covering clothes cut the heat lost from the body, so there is less to make up by shivering.

overlay.caption: cold air → shiver and pull blood from the skin (fades indoors) · UV from sky + snow → redness hours later

explain.summary: Elif's skin had two separate things happen to it. The freezing, windy air pulled heat out of her fast, so her muscles shivered to make heat and blood was kept away from her skin — all of which fades within minutes by the fire. Meanwhile UV from the sky, doubled by snow reflecting it back up, was damaging her skin cells; that shows up as redness hours later, and peeling days later.
rules: Wind chill uses the National Weather Service formula: colder air and stronger wind take heat faster.
Shivering grows as the wind chill drops below about 40 °F; warm clothes and a hat reduce it.
UV reaching her face = hours outside × UV index × the snow boost, minus what sunscreen blocks.
Redness appears once the UV passes what her skin can take, and grows from there.
The cold effects end when she warms up; the UV damage has already been done.

source.fact: Snow reflects up to 80% of the sun's UV light, so the rays hit you twice; UV can burn skin year-round, especially at high altitudes.
The first signs of sunburn may not appear for a few hours; the full effect may take 24 hours; peeling comes several days later; reflections off snow make the sun's rays stronger.
The UV Index rates UV strength; at 3 or more, protection is needed.
Wind chill is based on the rate of heat loss from exposed skin caused by wind and cold: Wind chill (°F) = 35.74 + 0.6215T − 35.75·V^0.16 + 0.4275T·V^0.16, for T in °F and wind V in mph.
Cold, wet or windy conditions can make the body lose more heat than it makes; shivering and chattering teeth are early signs.
Shivering is rapid, repeated muscle contractions that release heat to warm us up.

choice.what: Snow adds 80% to the UV on her face
choice.why: Uses the 'up to 80%' reflection figure; real boosts depend on how fresh the snow is and which way she faces.

choice.what: Shivering grows by 1 point for every 5 °F of wind chill below 40 °F
choice.why: Gives strong shivering at a 9 °F wind chill with no hat; the real starting point varies between people.

choice.what: Shivering builds up over the first hour outside
choice.why: Bodies cool gradually; after about an hour the shivering is steady.
Well-applied sunscreen blocks more, but people usually put on less than the label assumes; this is a teaching value.

choice.what: Narrower skin blood vessels are shown as falling skin blood flow
choice.why: Keeping warm blood away from the skin is the body's heat-saving move; the size here is a teaching scale.

illustrative: Elif's five hours, the UV index of 3, 20 °F with a 10 mph wind and her 'sometimes burns' skin are made up for a fictional story.
Burn units and the 0–10 redness and shivering scales are teaching scales.

citations.title: Winter Sun Safety
citations.supports: Snow reflects up to 80 percent of the sun's UV light, so the rays hit you twice; UVB can burn and damage skin year-round, especially at high altitudes.

citations.title: Sunburn
citations.supports: First signs of sunburn may not appear for a few hours and the full effect can take 24 hours or more; peeling follows several days later; reflections off water, sand or snow make the sun's burning rays stronger.

citations.title: UV Index Scale
citations.supports: UV Index 1–2 low (minimal protection); 3–7 moderate to high (protection needed); 8+ very high to extreme (extra protection needed).

citations.title: Wind Chill Chart
citations.supports: Wind chill is based on the rate of heat loss from exposed skin caused by wind and cold; formula 35.74 + 0.6215T − 35.75(V^0.16) + 0.4275T(V^0.16), valid at or below 50 °F and winds above 3 mph.

citations.title: Hypothermia (Low Body Temperature)
citations.supports: Hypothermia happens after exposure to cold, wet or windy conditions that make the body lose more heat than it generates; shivering and chattering teeth are early signs.

citations.title: Curious Kids: why do we shiver when we feel cold?
citations.supports: Shivering is rapid, repeated contraction of muscles; it produces no useful movement but releases heat that helps warm us up.

does: Shows two separate effects on the same skin, each with its own timing
Uses the National Weather Service wind chill formula for the cold
Shows snow boosting UV and sunscreen cutting it
doesnt: Measure any real person — Elif is fictional and the scales are for teaching
Account for time of day, altitude, clouds, or skin tone in detail
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: Numb, white or hard patches of skin in the cold, or blistering after sun, are reasons to tell an adult straight away.
